In that time, you could, say, walk out of a dangerous situation or reposition everyone’s weapons out of their hands. It’s essentially a super-buffer or reset button. Alternatively, a limited rewind ability could undo a round of combat – say an ally got hurt or killed, you rewind to before that happened and choose a different action (preventing the fight from turning deadly). Time manipulation is special since it can prevent outcomes that have already started to occur. Example: bandits spring an ambush and fire crossbows, you freeze time, move all the bolts aside (or mark their trajectories) and unfreeze – their volley misses completely, maybe scaring them (divine intervention vibe) and avoiding the fight. Or an argument leading to a duel – you rewind a few moments and interject with wiser words to stop the duel challenge from ever being issued.

synergies: Time Stop + Rescue/Disarm: freeze time, then do non-violent actions like grabbing all weapons, pulling people out of harm’s way, etc., resume time and conflict likely fizzles (“Our swords vanished What sorcery! We yield.”). Slow (as in debuff) + Haste (buff) are minor time warps that we covered – not full stop but relative control, making one side effectively experiencing longer time than the other, which can stop conflict quickly because one side can’t react. Time Reversal + Knowledge: if you have foresight or post-cognition, you can alter events – e.g., see that talking will break down into fight at minute X, so you rewind to before that and take a different approach. It’s a narrative synergy where time magic plus insight can make you an ultimate conflict avoider – you trial-and-error through time loops until you find the peaceful path (like “Edge of Tomorrow” but used to find a diplomatic solution instead of a perfect combat run). Time Dilation + Escape: you could trap foes in a bubble where time flows super slow – by the time they get out, you and innocents are long gone (no fight). Or vice versa, speed up an evacuation relative to attackers. Time Stop + Healing: if someone is about to die from wounds, stop time to perform emergency care (which might normally take many rounds or minutes but you do it in an eye-blink from outside perspective). That's special as in preventing a casualty (which could spur revenge cycles). Overuse of time manipulation might be narrative-breaking, but in one-off critical moments, it’s the ultimate special ability to say “No violence today, let’s reset.” And interestingly, two sides with time powers could get into a war that never actually progresses (“I undo your strike” “I freeze you before you strike” etc., until they hopefully realize fighting is pointless). So, time control is an extreme but potent tool in the non-combat toolbox, often concluding conflicts through deus ex machina style pacification.

abilities.name: Transmutation (Material Transformation)
abilities.description: Magically changing one material or element into another or altering its properties. A transmuter focuses on spells like Transmute Rock to Mud, Water to Wine, Stone Shape, etc. They can turn a solid wall into mud to create a passage, or vice-versa solidify water into ice for a bridge. In Fullmetal Alchemist (a novel/manga example), practitioners abide by Equivalent Exchange – “to create something, something of equal value must be lost” – but they routinely reshape metal, earth, etc. One common transmutation in fantasy literature is turning lead into gold (the alchemical pinnacle). Another is Polymorphing others into different forms (though that borders on a combat effect if used offensively). Non-combat uses include: reinforcing a collapsing cave by transmuting sand to stone, reshaping a broken key to work again, or turning raw materials into finished ones (wood -> wooden ladder).

abilities.description: A combat technique that sweeps an opponent’s legs or otherwise throws them off-balance, causing them to fall prone. A tripped enemy on the ground has difficulty moving and defending – attackers get an easier shot while they’re down. In ancient textsterms, a Battlemaster fighter’s Trip Attack maneuver forces a target to make a Strength save or be knocked prone. While prone, the target’s movement is halved and melee hits against them are often at advantage (since they’re struggling to get up). This ability doesn’t injure directly, but it controls the enemy’s position, setting them up for follow-up attacks or forcing them to spend time recovering instead of fighting.

abilities.name: Water Manipulation
abilities.description: Control over water and liquids – moving water, changing its shape, or even its state (to some extent, like freezing or vaporizing small amounts). A hydromancer can do things like: draw water from a well without a bucket (make it rise to you), split and part water (like creating a temporary dry path in a stream to cross it), or condense moisture from the air into a usable supply. Non-combat uses are extensive: dousing fires, purifying water (by separating sediment), irrigating crops by channeling river water, or creating sculptures and tools from ice. Underwater breathing could be achieved indirectly (wrap a bubble of air around someone’s head using water/air control). Travel can be aided by water shaping too – for instance, propelling a boat by forming a current.

details.name: Water Manipulation
details.description: Control over water and liquids – moving water, changing its shape, or even its state (to some extent, like freezing or vaporizing small amounts). A hydromancer can do things like: draw water from a well without a bucket (make it rise to you), split and part water (like creating a temporary dry path in a stream to cross it), or condense moisture from the air into a usable supply. Non-combat uses are extensive: dousing fires, purifying water (by separating sediment), irrigating crops by channeling river water, or creating sculptures and tools from ice. Underwater breathing could be achieved indirectly (wrap a bubble of air around someone’s head using water/air control). Travel can be aided by water shaping too – for instance, propelling a boat by forming a current.

synergies: Water is the classic combo element. Water + Lightning yields an electrified water effect – e.g., in Divinity: Original Sin, “water + lightning = electrified water, which stuns anyone in it”. So a water manipulator can spread a conductive layer and an ally’s lightning can then incapacitate multiple foes – a tactical synergy. Water + Cold (with either innate freezing ability or an ally with ice magic) can create ice – you might flood an area then freeze it to seal a door or form an ice bridge. Water + Earth makes mud, as noted – a water mage could soften the ground under an enemy’s feet into mud, and if an earth mage then hardens it, the foe’s legs might be stuck. For non-combat synergy: Water + Plant manipulation – nurturing plants via irrigation, or conversely, water can wash away harmful salt from soil while a plant mage encourages growth. Additionally, Water + Gravity could purify or separate liquids (heavy impurities sink faster in increased gravity water). With Fire, it’s usually oppositional (steam as a side effect or extinguishing each other), but a clever combination can produce steam power or even a thick fog (heat water into fog for concealment). Essentially, water’s versatility allows it to collaborate with nearly any other element for creative problem-solving.

abilities.name: Weakness (Enfeeblement)
abilities.description: A curse or effect that saps the physical strength or effectiveness of a target. An example is Ray of Enfeeblement, a spell that causes a creature’s strength-based attacks to do half damage – essentially their blows land with far less force because their muscles weaken. Another example: a potion of weakness in Skyrim makes an enemy take more damage or deal less damage. Non-combat wise, you could use this to subdue a strong opponent without injuring them – e.g., enfeeble a raging barbarian so that when they hit, it’s like a child hitting, allowing you to restrain or talk sense into them. It’s also handy for labor situations: prevent a hostile giant from lifting a boulder to throw it by zapping them with weakness so they drop it. If someone is using strength to break something (door, chains), enfeeble them to delay or prevent it. It is a targeted debuff that doesn’t immobilize, but significantly reduces physical threat.

details.name: Weakness (Enfeeblement)
details.description: A curse or effect that saps the physical strength or effectiveness of a target. An example is Ray of Enfeeblement, a spell that causes a creature’s strength-based attacks to do half damage – essentially their blows land with far less force because their muscles weaken. Another example: a potion of weakness in Skyrim makes an enemy take more damage or deal less damage. Non-combat wise, you could use this to subdue a strong opponent without injuring them – e.g., enfeeble a raging barbarian so that when they hit, it’s like a child hitting, allowing you to restrain or talk sense into them. It’s also handy for labor situations: prevent a hostile giant from lifting a boulder to throw it by zapping them with weakness so they drop it. If someone is using strength to break something (door, chains), enfeeble them to delay or prevent it. It is a targeted debuff that doesn’t immobilize, but significantly reduces physical threat.

synergies: Enfeeblement + Disarm: a weak enemy can’t resist a disarm attempt well – they have no strength to hold their weapon, making it easier to pluck away (mechanics aside, narratively that fits). Weakness + Grapple: if you enfeeble an opponent, even a smaller person could grapple and hold them because the target’s strength contest is poor – a means to capture someone alive safely. Weakness + Protection: combining weakening a foe and casting protective buffs on allies ensures that even if the foe tries to fight, they likely can’t hurt anyone – a great non-lethal outcome where the foe tires out punching your armored, blessed, hearty self and eventually gives up. Weakness + Negotiation: show a brute that their strength means nothing (by magically weakening them mid-brawl) and they might lose the will to fight, making them more amenable to talks. Weakness + Empower (on different targets): a dramatization – you weaken the enemy’s champion while subtly enhancing the allied champion (maybe via Bless or Giant’s Strength potion) – when they duel, the enemy’s side is likely to yield seeing their champion easily bested, resolving a larger conflict. Also, Weakness vs. creatures reliant on strength (like a pack animal or a siege ogre) can halt an impending non-human threat – e.g., an enfeebled dragon might struggle to take off or break through a gate, buying time for a peaceful evacuation or a ritual. Essentially, Weakness-type debuffs are a way to remove the “might makes right” factor from an equation – if the bully or monster no longer has overwhelming strength, alternative solutions and dialogues often emerge.

abilities.name: Weather Control
abilities.description: A grand ability to influence the weather patterns over an area. This includes summoning rain, storms, fog, wind, or calming such weather. A druid or powerful sorcerer might cast Control Weather, which over ~10 minutes can change weather conditions (within natural limits for the region/season) – e.g., calling a thunderstorm on a summer day or a blizzard in winter. They can’t pinpoint things like exactly where lightning will strike, but they control the general trend (wind direction, precipitation, temperature). Non-combat uses: end a drought by bringing rain (or create a downpour to douse a widespread fire), ensure safe passage for a ship by invoking a favorable wind and clear skies, or conversely, cover a retreat with heavy fog or a sudden snowstorm. Weather control can prevent natural disasters (calm a hurricane) or unfortunately cause them (though causing would often be combative or at least hostile to someone). It’s a wide-area, strategic ability rather than tactical.

details.name: Weather Control
details.description: A grand ability to influence the weather patterns over an area. This includes summoning rain, storms, fog, wind, or calming such weather. A druid or powerful sorcerer might cast Control Weather, which over ~10 minutes can change weather conditions (within natural limits for the region/season) – e.g., calling a thunderstorm on a summer day or a blizzard in winter. They can’t pinpoint things like exactly where lightning will strike, but they control the general trend (wind direction, precipitation, temperature). Non-combat uses: end a drought by bringing rain (or create a downpour to douse a widespread fire), ensure safe passage for a ship by invoking a favorable wind and clear skies, or conversely, cover a retreat with heavy fog or a sudden snowstorm. Weather control can prevent natural disasters (calm a hurricane) or unfortunately cause them (though causing would often be combative or at least hostile to someone). It’s a wide-area, strategic ability rather than tactical.

synergies: Weather control is basically combining Air, Water, and sometimes Lightning on a large scale. If you have lesser elemental abilities, controlling weather might amplify them: e.g., an air mage and water mage working in concert could mimic a limited weather control – one brings clouds, the other directs winds and pressure. If one can control weather and another has Lightning magic, you could guarantee strikes by providing constant storm conditions for the lightning caster to draw from (some games require a storm present to call lightning, for example). Weather + Agriculture: a nature/plant mage could ensure crops get perfect amounts of rain and sun by coordinating with the weather mage – literally ending hunger in a region by optimizing weather for growth. On adventures, Weather + Stealth: you might summon a dark storm to give cover of night early, or heavy rain to mask sound and sight while the party infiltrates. Weather + Mood: interestingly, weather can affect morale – combined with Emotional Control, a sudden sunny day can lift spirits, or a gloomy drizzle can prep people for a somber mood (funeral magic). Also, Weather + Sea travel synergy is classic – one ensures calm seas or tailwinds, greatly reducing travel time or avoiding deadly storms (which in a campaign can skip random encounters at sea – a non-combat outcome indeed!). Essentially, controlling weather on demand is almost like having a deity’s influence – it can avert whole categories of danger (floods, droughts, sandstorms) and facilitate events (festivals in good weather, etc.). It’s the ultimate “environment hack” to shape the world to suit the party’s needs.
